question:
Patient note:
A 55-year-old man with a remote history of injection-drug use that led to chronic hepatitis C genotype 1b—treated three years ago with ledipasvir/sofosbuvir but leaving behind biopsy-proven stage 4 fibrosis and small esophageal varices last surveyed eight months ago—walked into the emergency department at 19:10 after noticing that his last two bowel movements were a thick, jet-black paste that clung to the porcelain and produced a sharp iron odor despite multiple flushes. Earlier in the afternoon he had finished a grilled beef sandwich at work, felt a vague epigastric heaviness, then passed what he thought was unusually dark stool; when a second passage four hours later looked “like roofing tar,” co-workers urged him to seek evaluation. He drove himself the twenty-five minutes to the hospital without needing to pull over, never experienced dimming vision, ear ringing, or a sensation of impending blackout, and states he was able to unload his toolbox from the truck bed without weakness or imbalance. Past medical problems apart from the treated viral hepatitis include well-controlled hypertension managed with lisinopril 10 mg daily and dyspepsia for which he takes over-the-counter omeprazole most mornings; he has never been told he has fluid around the lungs or heart, has no exertional limitations, and bicycles eight miles every weekend without breathlessness. He denies ever having required diuretics, nitrates, or echocardiographic follow-up for a weakened ventricle. Medications are limited to lisinopril, omeprazole, and a daily multivitamin; he takes no non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, anticoagulants, antiplatelet agents, corticosteroids, or herbal supplements. He stopped drinking alcohol five years ago, has not used illicit drugs since antiviral therapy, smokes half a pack of cigarettes per day, and works full-time as a metal fabricator. Family history reveals a father with myocardial infarction at 70 and a brother with type 2 diabetes; there are no inherited bleeding disorders. Review of systems performed at triage is negative for fever, chills, cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, leg swelling, jaundice beyond his baseline faint scleral tint, pruritus, abdominal distention, hematemesis, bright red blood per rectum, hematuria, or unintentional weight change. On presentation—prior to placement of any intravenous catheter, administration of fluids, vasoactive medication, blood products, proton-pump inhibitor, octreotide, or antiemetic—he sat upright on the stretcher, calm, conversant, and oriented, holding a sealed plastic bag containing a tissue streaked with glossy midnight stool as evidence for staff. A calibrated manual sphygmomanometer on the left arm supported at heart level recorded a blood pressure of 160 / 96 mm Hg, and the bedside monitor simultaneously displayed a regular sinus rhythm at 67 beats per minute that matched a bounding radial pulse; respirations were 16 per minute, oral temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air. Capillary refill was two seconds, conjunctivae were only mildly pale, sclerae exhibited a chronic subtle icteric hue, and oral mucosa was moist without telangiectasias or petechiae. Neck veins were not distended at 45°, carotid upstrokes were brisk without bruits, and peripheral pulses were full and symmetric without edema. Cardiac auscultation revealed crisp S1 and S2 without murmurs, gallops, or rubs. Lung fields were clear to percussion and auscultation bilaterally. The abdomen was flat, soft, and non-distended; gentle palpation elicited mild tenderness in the left upper quadrant but no rebound, guarding, hepatosplenomegaly, or palpable masses. There was no shifting dullness or fluid wave. Spider angiomas numbering fewer than a dozen dotted the anterior chest, and faint palmar erythema was noted, but the skin was otherwise free of ecchymoses or purpura. A focused neurologic screen showed equal reactive pupils, intact extraocular movements, 5/5 strength in all extremities, steady gait when asked to stand, and no asterixis. After informed consent a single 20-gauge catheter was inserted in the right antecubital vein strictly for diagnostic sampling and type-and-screen; at that precise moment he had received no therapy of any kind. Stat laboratory studies drawn through that line returned within twelve minutes, still prior to any intervention: hemoglobin 15.5 g/dL, hematocrit 46 %, mean corpuscular volume 90 fL, platelet count 132 × 10⁹/L, white-blood-cell count 6.9 × 10⁹/L, blood urea nitrogen 84 mg/dL, serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL (baseline 1.1), sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 106 mg/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.2; alanine aminotransferase, aspartate aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, albumin, and ammonia were pending. A 12-lead electrocardiogram obtained simultaneously demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 68 bpm with age-appropriate R-wave progression and no acute ST-segment deviations. Upright chest radiography revealed clear lung fields and a normal cardiomediastinal silhouette, while a single supine abdominal radiograph showed a non-specific gas pattern without evidence of obstruction or free intraperitoneal air. A digital rectal examination performed immediately afterward produced a gloved finger coated in thick, tarry stool that turned the guaiac card deep blue within seconds. He remains fasting, attached to continuous cardiac and pulse-oximetry monitoring in the resuscitation bay, while gastroenterology is paged for urgent endoscopic evaluation of his suspected upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage occurring in the setting of chronic hepatic parenchymal disease and significant azotemia, all before any resuscitative or pharmacologic measures have begun.

Question: What is the patient's Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Glasgow-Blatchford Bleeding Score uses admission urea, sex-specific hemoglobin, systolic pressure, pulse, melena, syncope, hepatic disease, and heart failure.
- Urea: BUN 84 mg/dL corresponds to urea 84/2.8 = 30 mmol/L. Urea ≥25 mmol/L → 6.
- Hemoglobin: 15.5 g/dL in a man is ≥13 → 0.
- Systolic pressure: 160 mm Hg is ≥110 → 0.
- Pulse: 67/min is <100 → 0.
- Melena: black, tarry stool confirmed on rectal exam → 1.
- Syncope: none → 0.
- Hepatic disease: biopsy-proven cirrhosis with varices despite hepatitis C treatment → 2.
- Heart failure: no history or findings → 0.
Total = 6 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 9.
Final answer: 9
